compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic analogue of alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone that binds mainly to the melanocortin-1 receptor and increases eumelanin in the skin. It is approved as a controlled-release subcutaneous implant (Scenesse) for adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP), a rare inherited condition causing painful reactions to light, in the US, EU, UK, Canada and Australia. The same molecule (Melanotan-1) is also sold as unapproved powder for cosmetic tanning; that material is not the approved product.

evidence.summary: Two multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCTs (74 patients in the EU, 94 in the US) found longer pain-free direct sunlight exposure with afamelanotide (US median 69.4 versus 40.8 hours over 6 months; EU median 6.0 versus 0.8 hours over 9 months) and improved quality of life. An observational study of 115 patients treated for up to 8 years at two centres reported sustained use and only minor adverse events. The EU authorisation is under exceptional circumstances because comprehensive data could not be obtained.

evidence.summary: The developer ran six randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in about 900 adults, mostly with obesity, by mouth or single intravenous doses. A review states that a 12-week trial showed modestly greater weight loss than placebo, but that development ended after a 24-week trial in 536 people failed to show significant weight loss. Rodent studies reported reduced weight gain and increased fat breakdown.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic 15-amino-acid peptide first described by a research group in Zagreb in 1993. It is sold widely on the gray market and through some clinics with claims of tendon, ligament, muscle and gut "healing". FDA's July 2026 briefing document states that no product containing it is approved in any country. Almost all published efficacy data are from rodent studies, most from a single research group; human data are limited to small uncontrolled reports and one trial reported only as a conference abstract.

evidence.indication: Tendon, ligament, muscle and joint injury
evidence.summary: The musculoskeletal claims rest on rat studies of cut or detached tendons, ligaments and muscles, nearly all from one Zagreb group. The only human report is a retrospective chart review with telephone follow-up of 16 clinic patients given intra-articular injections for knee pain of mixed causes, some with a second peptide; it had no control group and no standardised outcome measure. No randomised or prospective controlled human study has been published. FDA's 2026 briefing document states that it did not identify clinical studies of BPC-157 for tendonitis. A placebo-controlled hamstring-strain trial and a rotator-cuff pilot trial are registered but have not reported.

evidence.indication: Raising GH and IGF-1 levels (pharmacodynamic marker, healthy adults)

A separate uncontrolled before-and-after study in healthy young men found raised trough and mean GH with preserved pulsatility, and higher IGF-1, one week after a single dose. These are small, short studies of a hormone marker, not of any clinical outcome.

Labelled uses include central diabetes insipidus, primary nocturnal enuresis, nocturia due to nocturnal polyuria, and, for the injectable form, certain bleeding disorders.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic four-residue peptide that binds cardiolipin, a lipid of the inner mitochondrial membrane. The US FDA granted it accelerated approval in September 2025 (brand Forzinity) for muscle strength in Barth syndrome, a rare inherited mitochondrial disease, on the basis of an intermediate endpoint, with a confirmatory trial required. It has also been tested in primary mitochondrial myopathy, dry macular degeneration and heart failure. Under the research name SS-31 it is also sold outside medical channels with anti-ageing and mitochondrial-health claims.

evidence.indication: Barth syndrome (muscle strength, exercise capacity, fatigue)
evidence.summary: The only controlled evidence is TAZPOWER, a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 12 males with Barth syndrome. In the randomised part neither primary endpoint (six-minute walk distance and a Barth symptom score) was met. In the open-label extension, without a concurrent control group, walk distance, symptom scores and knee extensor strength improved from baseline. FDA's accelerated approval rests on knee extensor strength, an intermediate endpoint, and FDA requires a randomised placebo-controlled confirmatory trial (registered as 4TAZPower).

The larger phase 3 trial (MMPOWER-3, 218 participants, 24 weeks) did not meet either primary endpoint; the between-group difference in walk distance was close to zero. compounds.sequence_note: An alternatively spliced isoform of human follistatin, a cysteine-rich secreted glycoprotein rather than a short peptide. Black-market products analysed in 2019 contained a His-tagged recombinant protein with a high proportion of oligomers.
compounds.what_it_is: A form of follistatin, a natural protein that binds and blocks myostatin and related growth factors that limit muscle growth. Gray-market vials labelled "follistatin 344" are sold for muscle building. That is different from the clinical research, which used a gene-therapy virus carrying the follistatin-344 gene, injected into the thigh muscles of a few patients with muscular dystrophy or inclusion body myositis. No follistatin product is approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked.

evidence.indication: Muscle growth and strength (injected follistatin-344 protein)
evidence.summary: No published study of injected follistatin-344 protein in any model, animal or human, was identified. Animal studies of follistatin protein used other forms: an engineered follistatin-315 fusion protein increased lean mass in mice, while follistatin-288 protein in rats had mixed effects, including smaller muscles and less force in some groups. These results cannot be transferred to gray-market follistatin-344, whose stability, activity and content are unknown.

In macaques, the same vector increased muscle size and strength.

compounds.sequence_note: Copper(II) complex of the tripeptide glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine (GHK). The peptide occurs naturally in human plasma.
compounds.what_it_is: A copper complex of a three-amino-acid peptide found naturally in human plasma. It is a common ingredient in topical cosmetic skin products and is also sold on the gray market as an injectable with anti-ageing and tissue-healing claims. A topical gel was tested for diabetic foot ulcers in the 1990s; no approval of it was identified. It is not an FDA-approved medicine, and in the US FDA treats injectable and non-injectable use separately for compounding.

evidence.summary: A multicentre, randomised, evaluator-blinded, vehicle-controlled trial of a GHK-copper gel (Iamin Gel) in diabetic neuropathic plantar ulcers, published in 1994, reported greater median ulcer closure and fewer infections than vehicle when added to standard wound care. The number of participants was not stated in the abstract reviewed. No confirmatory trial was identified, and no approval of the gel was found.

Other published cosmetic studies mostly test multi-ingredient products, so the contribution of GHK-Cu cannot be isolated.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic six-amino-acid peptide, one of the first growth hormone secretagogues, which acts on the ghrelin receptor to release growth hormone from the pituitary. It was studied widely in human endocrine physiology experiments in the 1990s but was never approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked. It is sold online as a research chemical with claims of raising growth hormone, appetite and muscle mass. A Cuban research centre has tested it with epidermal growth factor in acute stroke.

evidence.summary: Many small, short human pharmacology studies, several of them randomised placebo-controlled crossover designs in healthy volunteers or patients, show that intravenous GHRP-6 acutely raises blood growth hormone, an effect that is greater when combined with GHRH and partly depends on endogenous GHRH. It also raised ACTH and cortisol. These studies measured hormone levels over hours; none tested sustained IGF-I, body composition, strength or any clinical outcome. The number of such studies was not counted, so both counts are left blank.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic six-amino-acid growth hormone secretagogue, a close analogue of GHRP-6, that acts on the ghrelin receptor to release growth hormone. It was studied in human endocrine experiments and small clinical studies in the 1990s, including in children with short stature and in adults over 16 weeks, but was never approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked. WADA lists it under the name examorelin. It is sold online as a research chemical with claims of raising growth hormone and muscle mass.

evidence.summary: Numerous small human pharmacology studies, many randomised and placebo-controlled with crossover designs, show that hexarelin acutely raises blood growth hormone after intravenous, subcutaneous, intranasal or oral administration, alongside rises in prolactin, ACTH and cortisol. In adults given hexarelin twice daily for 16 weeks the growth hormone response was partly and reversibly attenuated, and IGF-I did not change significantly. The number of such studies was not counted, so both counts are left blank.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic five-residue peptide that stimulates growth hormone release by acting on the ghrelin (growth hormone secretagogue) receptor. It was developed by Novo Nordisk in the 1990s and later tested by Helsinn as an intravenous treatment for postoperative ileus, where its published Phase 2 trial did not meet its efficacy endpoints. It is not approved anywhere checked and has no active sponsor. It is sold as a "research chemical" with claims of muscle gain, fat loss, recovery, sleep and "anti-ageing".

evidence.indication: Muscle gain, fat loss, recovery, sleep and anti-ageing (gray-market claims)
evidence.summary: No human study has tested any of these outcomes. Human data are limited to a pharmacokinetic study in healthy men showing a single, short-lived rise in growth hormone after intravenous infusion. In mice, ipamorelin increased body fat rather than reducing it, an effect the authors attributed to GH-independent mechanisms such as increased feeding. Raised hormone levels are a laboratory measure, not evidence of muscle gain, fat loss or any health benefit.

It is used as a research tool in human reproductive-physiology studies. It is not approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked, and it is sold on the gray market with claims of raising testosterone and libido. These studies measured hormone levels over hours; none tested symptoms, sexual function, body composition or any clinical outcome, and none lasted weeks or months. Whether any of the designs were randomised was not verified, so the RCT count is left blank. No trial of repeated self-administered kisspeptin-10 in hypogonadism was identified.

Labelled uses include advanced prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids (with iron, before surgery) and central precocious puberty, varying by product and jurisdiction.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic cyclic peptide related to alpha-melanocyte-stimulating hormone that activates several melanocortin receptors. It was studied in small academic trials in the 1990s for tanning and erectile function, then not developed as a medicine. It is not approved anywhere checked and is sold online as an unlicensed injectable "tanning" product. Its documented human record is dominated by case reports of harm: changing and new moles, melanoma, priapism, rhabdomyolysis and kidney injury.

evidence.summary: The only published efficacy data are a pilot phase 1 study in three healthy men (single-blind, alternating days of injection and saline) in which two subjects showed increased facial and body pigmentation. No randomised trial of tanning has been published. No study has tested whether induced tanning reduces sunburn or skin cancer, and case reports describe new and changing moles in users.

evidence.summary: Small double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies from a single US research group in the late 1990s reported erections after injection more often than after placebo, in men with psychogenic and with organic erectile dysfunction, and higher self-rated sexual desire. In the organic study, 12 of 19 injections initiated erections versus 1 of 21 placebo doses, and 4 of 19 injections caused severe nausea. No larger trial has been published.

compounds.what_it_is: A 16-amino-acid peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA and found naturally in human blood and muscle. A synthetic version is sold on the gray market with claims of weight loss, better insulin sensitivity, exercise performance and longevity. It is not approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked. FDA states it has identified no human exposure data for products containing it by any route. The World Anti-Doping Agency names it as a prohibited metabolic modulator.

evidence.indication: Obesity, weight loss and insulin resistance
evidence.summary: The founding study reported that MOTS-c treatment in mice prevented diet-induced obesity and age-related and diet-induced insulin resistance. No published human trial of MOTS-c for weight, glucose control or insulin sensitivity was identified. A placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in adults with prediabetes was registered in China in 2026 and is recruiting, with no results. A company-developed analogue (CB4211) completed a phase 1 trial, but that is a different molecule and its results were not identified in a peer-reviewed journal.

No human trial of administered MOTS-c for exercise capacity, muscle function or ageing outcomes was identified.

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic eight-residue cyclic analogue of the hormone somatostatin, with a longer half-life than the native hormone. It is an approved prescription drug in the United States and Canada in short-acting and long-acting injectable forms, and in the United States as an oral delayed-release capsule. Labelled uses centre on acromegaly and on symptoms of carcinoid and other hormone-secreting neuroendocrine tumours.

evidence.summary: Injectable octreotide has been used in acromegaly since the late 1980s, largely on the basis of uncontrolled and open-label studies. The oral capsule was tested in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial (OPTIMAL, 56 participants) in people already controlled on injectable somatostatin analogues, and in an open-label randomised non-inferiority trial against injectables (MPOWERED). One adequately designed placebo-controlled RCT is cited here; the outcome is a biochemical marker (IGF-I), not tumour or survival outcomes.

No overall survival benefit was established in the primary report. This indication is not part of the US label wording for octreotide.

compounds.what_it_is: A seven-amino-acid peptide cut down from spadin, a fragment of the propeptide released when the sorting protein sortilin matures. It was designed in a French laboratory as a blocker of the TREK-1 potassium channel and tested for antidepressant-like activity in mice. It is sold online as a research chemical with claims for depression, mood and cognition. No study in humans was identified and no approved medicine contains it.

evidence.summary: Efficacy data are from mice only. In the 2017 report that introduced it, PE 22-28 reduced immobility in the forced swim test, shortened escape latency in a learned-helplessness test and reduced feeding latency in a novelty-suppressed feeding test, including in a corticosterone-induced depression model, with a longer-lasting effect than its parent peptide spadin. These are behavioural screening tests in mice; no human study of mood, depression or any other outcome was identified.

compounds.what_it_is: An investigational synthetic peptide from Eli Lilly that activates three hormone receptors: GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon. It is in phase 3 development for obesity, type 2 diabetes and related conditions. It is not approved in any jurisdiction checked. The UK MHRA states it is not authorised and that products sold under the name are sold illegally; case reports describe harm after use of online-purchased material.

evidence.indication: Weight reduction in obesity or overweight (the main use it is sold for)

TRIUMPH-1 (2,339 adults without diabetes, 80 weeks): mean weight change -17.6% to -25.0% across dose groups versus -3.9% with placebo. TRIUMPH-2 (1,152 adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes, 80 weeks): -11.9% to -18.8% versus -5.1%. The phase 2 trial (338 adults, 48 weeks) reported -8.7% to -24.2% versus -2.1%. Phase 3 results of TRIUMPH-3 and TRIUMPH-4 (both completed on ClinicalTrials.gov) were not located in a publication.

evidence.summary: Three small Russian clinical studies were identified, none placebo-controlled. In 62 patients with generalised anxiety disorder or neurasthenia, selank and the benzodiazepine medazepam had similar anxiolytic effects. In 60 patients with anxiety and somatoform disorders, selank was compared with phenazepam. In 70 patients, adding selank to phenazepam was reported to bring an earlier response and fewer benzodiazepine side effects. PubMed indexes two of these as randomised; the designs were not verified from full texts, so the RCT count is left blank. Without placebo arms these studies cannot separate drug effect from the high placebo response typical of anxiety trials.

evidence.summary: Supported by a large phase 3 programme. In SUSTAIN-6 (3,297 people with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk), major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 6.6% on semaglutide versus 8.9% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.74). In FLOW (3,533 people with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease), the composite kidney and cardiovascular outcome was 24% lower with semaglutide (hazard ratio 0.76); the trial stopped early for efficacy.

evidence.summary: Multiple large placebo-controlled trials (the STEP programme). Discontinuation for adverse events was about twice as common with semaglutide (16.6% vs 8.2%).

compounds.what_it_is: A synthetic seven-amino-acid fragment of thymosin beta-4, a 43-residue protein found in most human cells. It is often marketed as if it were thymosin beta-4 itself, with claims of faster recovery from tendon, ligament and muscle injuries and wound healing. Research on the full-length protein does not transfer automatically to the fragment. TB-500 is not approved as a medicine in any jurisdiction checked. FDA states it has identified no human exposure data for it, and the World Anti-Doping Agency names it as prohibited.

No study of the fragment in tendon, ligament or muscle injury models was identified. No published human trial of TB-500 exists. A phase 1/2 trial of the fragment for cardiovascular biomarkers was registered in China in 2026 and is recruiting, with no results; it does not address injury recovery.

evidence.summary: Two large randomised controlled trials with fracture endpoints support this approved indication. In the pivotal placebo-controlled trial of 1,637 postmenopausal women with prior vertebral fracture, teriparatide reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fragility fractures and increased bone mineral density. In VERO, a double-blind trial of 1,360 women with severe osteoporosis, new vertebral fractures were less frequent with teriparatide than with the active comparator risedronate. Reduction of hip fracture has not been demonstrated (EMA product overview).

compounds.sequence_note: 28 residues with an acetylated N-terminal serine; corresponds to residues 2-29 of human prothymosin alpha (UniProt P06454).
compounds.what_it_is: A 28-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from thymus tissue, made synthetically as thymalfasin (brand Zadaxin). It is an approved prescription medicine in some countries, mainly for chronic hepatitis B and as an immune adjunct, but is not approved in the United States. FDA states it is not approved in the US, Japan or Europe except Italy. In the US it is sold through compounding and gray-market channels with claims for viral infections, chronic fatigue, Lyme disease, cancer and general immune support.

evidence.summary: Several small randomised trials, mostly from the 1990s, gave mixed results. A Taiwanese trial of 98 patients reported higher combined viral clearance at 18 months with a 26-week course than with no treatment. A US phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 97 patients did not show a statistically significant difference. A meta-analysis of four small trials against interferon alpha found responses accumulated after treatment ended. FDA's 2024 review judged the evidence insufficient, noting outdated comparators and assays; none of the trials tested current standard antivirals as comparators.

A small earlier placebo-controlled pilot reported no viral clearance. These trials used older interferon regimens, not current direct-acting antivirals.

evidence.summary: The largest trial, TESTS (1,106 adults with sepsis in 22 Chinese centres, double-blind, placebo-controlled), found no difference in 28-day mortality (23.4% versus 24.1%). An earlier single-blind randomised trial (ETASS, 361 patients) reported lower 28-day mortality with a marginal p-value. The randomised evidence is therefore conflicting, and the larger, better-blinded trial was negative. All trials were conducted in China.

evidence.summary: A randomised trial in 488 patients with metastatic melanoma compared dacarbazine plus interferon alpha with arms adding thymosin alpha-1. More tumour responses were seen in two thymosin arms, but the differences in overall and progression-free survival did not reach statistical significance. FDA's 2024 review of liver and lung cancer studies found small randomised trials, single-arm and retrospective studies, and concluded the evidence was insufficient. These regimens are not current standard care.

evidence.indication: Type 2 diabetes: glycaemic control and cardiovascular outcomes
evidence.summary: Supported by the phase 3 SURPASS programme. In SURPASS-2 (1,879 participants on metformin), all tirzepatide doses lowered HbA1c more than semaglutide (differences -0.15 to -0.45 percentage points). In SURPASS-CVOT (13,299 participants with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease), tirzepatide was non-inferior to dulaglutide for major cardiovascular events (12.2% vs 13.1%, hazard ratio 0.92); superiority was not shown.

In SURMOUNT-5 (751 adults without diabetes), weight change at week 72 was -20.2% with tirzepatide versus -13.7% with semaglutide. Gastrointestinal events were the most common adverse events in SURMOUNT-5.

evidence.summary: One phase 3 trial (SUMMIT, 731 patients, median follow-up 104 weeks). Cardiovascular death or worsening heart failure occurred in 9.9% with tirzepatide versus 15.3% with placebo (hazard ratio 0.62). The difference was driven by worsening heart-failure events; cardiovascular deaths were few (8 vs 5) and did not differ.
